newsitem.title: USA: Closing arguments given in Oklahoma bombing case.
newsitem.headline: Closing arguments given in Oklahoma bombing case.

text.p: Timothy McVeigh bombed the federal building in Oklahoma City out of rage at the U.S. government, believing his attack would inspire a violent uprising in America, the prosecution said on Thursday at his trial.

In his closing argument, prosecutor Larry Mackey said evidence clearly proved McVeigh was responsible for the April 19, 1995 blast at the Alfred P. Murrah building that killed 168 people and wounded more than 500 others.
"Suddenly many lives were ended, and many, many more were changed forever," Mackey said. "America stood in shock. ... Who could do such a thing?"
"Based on the evidence, the answer is clear. Tim McVeigh did it," he said.
McVeigh, 29, faced the death penalty if convicted of federal murder and conspiracy charges. He did not testify in the trial.

Wearing a blue plaid shirt, khaki pants and his hair in a crewcut, McVeigh sat in the crowded courtroom and appeared to be listening intently. His brow was furrowed and he rested his chin on his hand.
Chief defence attorney Stephen Jones began his closing argument by asking the jurors to set aside their emotions in deciding McVeigh's fate.
The prosecution used sympathy for the victims and "repugnance" for McVeigh's extreme right-wing political views to present its case, he said.
Jones also asked the jurors if they had the courage to find McVeigh innocent. "Timothy McVeigh was convicted in the court of public opinion" long before his trial began, he said.
Jury deliberations were set to begin after closing arguments and final instructions from the judge.
In an argument that lasted for three hours and 15 minutes in the morning, the prosecutor painstakingly reviewed the government's evidence against McVeigh.

Mackey described how McVeigh allegedly purchased the bomb's ingredients, rented lockers for storage, bought a how-to book on building bombs, dropped off a getaway car, enlisted the help of co-conspirator Terry Nichols and drove to Oklahoma City to survey his intended target.
Nichols will be tried separately.

"The government has presented a smorgasbord of evidence. You can pick and choose," Mackey said. "You can push away entirely satisfied that the government has proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt."
He said the 168 people who died in the Murrah building blast were neither "tyrants" nor "stormtroopers" -- words McVeigh allegedly used in writings and comments to friends.

"They were bosses and secretaries, blacks and whites, mothers and daughters, fathers and sons," Mackey said. "They were a community. Contrast that for a moment with what you have come to know about Timothy McVeigh."

McVeigh's rage was prompted by the government's 1993 siege at the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas, where some 80 people died, the prosecutor said. The siege became a rallying cry for the right wing who believe the federal government overstepped its role as laid out in the U.S. Constitution.
McVeigh hoped his attack would trigger more violence against the government, Mackey said, adding "Tim McVeigh was wrong about America. He was wrong about America's response."

The prosecutor told the jury McVeigh was inspired by "The Turner Diaries," a novel about the violent overthrow of the U.S. governemnt by a band of right-wing extremists. But he said McVeigh was not on trial for his views.
"In America, everyone has a right to their beliefs. ... This is a murder case," Mackey said.

He defended the prosecution's star witnesses, Michael and Lori Fortier, who testified that McVeigh told them of the bombing in advance. Defence attorneys portrayed them as an irresponsible couple who lied in hopes of selling their story.
"Tim McVeigh has presented the Fortiers as morally corrupt drug abusers. Not too long ago, they were his friends," Mackey said.
